newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Japan's trade complaints office takes to the road.
newsitem.headline: Japan's trade complaints office takes to the road.

text.p: Japan's trade ombudsman is taking to the road to explain to foreign exporters how best to complain about any problems in penetrating the Japanese market.

Office of Trade and Investment Ombudsman (OTO) officials are in Europe this week to tell governments and business chiefs how the department works and boast of its success since it was established in 1982.
It has handled a total of 545 grievances, but the number of cases reaching it has been whittled down from around 50 a year to just two in 1996.
OTO chief Yoshio Okawara told Reuters that the office would exist for as long as a perception remained that Japanese markets were unfairly closed.
The office does not handle complaints regarding tariffs or other barriers that exist because of World Trade Organisation regulations or other trade agareements.
But it aims to help foreign companies to understand and overcome Japanese internal regulations such as standards and certification.

An example was a complaint by a U.S. mobile home maker that it was denied access to Japan. Because mobile homes were relatively unknown in Japan, officials assessed them as both vehicles and dwellings, and thus they could not be certified.
The OTO, which reports directly to the Japanese prime minister eventually managed to change the law so that they could be assessed separately.
The OTO says that just 149 of the 545 complaints have resulted in no change to market access. In the rest, it says, improvements have been made or misunderstandings cleared up.
The United States leads the number of complaints with 164 followed by the European Union with 158.
Anyone -- governments, businesses or individuals -- can file a complaint by filling out a form and sending it to any Japanese Trade mission around the world.
Okawara said OTO procedure had been speeded up so that the average "life" of a complaint was now less than three months.
"The system is not perfect...It can never be," he said. "But I believe the OTO has served a valuable role which is helping Japan's markets open to foreign goods."
